questions.q: Why must a payment API require an idempotency key on charge requests?
options: The keys let the gateway route each request to the correct region
Keys encrypt card data end to end during transit
Keys order concurrent charges from the same customer
Retried requests can be recognized and not charged twice
questions.explanation: Networks time out ambiguously, so clients must retry; the key lets the server recognize a repeat of an already-executed charge and return the original result instead of moving money again.

questions.q: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction:
options: Writes balanced debit and credit entries whose sums match
Updates a single running balance column atomically
Creates exactly one immutable log line for every account touched
Locks both accounts until end-of-day settlement
questions.explanation: Money always moves from somewhere to somewhere, so debits must equal credits. That invariant is checkable, which is what makes the ledger auditable and self-validating.

questions.q: What is a PSP (payment service provider) in a typical e-commerce flow?
options: The government regulator that audits merchant transaction records annually
The service that processes cards and moves funds on the merchant's behalf
The customer's issuing bank that approves each purchase
A fraud-scoring vendor consulted after settlement
questions.explanation: The PSP sits between the merchant and the card networks and banks, handling authorization, capture, settlement, and compliance so the merchant does not integrate with each bank directly.

questions.q: Why do PSPs deliver payment outcomes via webhooks in addition to API responses?
options: Webhooks are encrypted while API responses are not
Card networks mandate webhook delivery for compliance
Outcomes can arrive after the original request completes or times out
Webhooks bypass the strict rate limits that would throttle API status polling
questions.explanation: Many events are asynchronous, such as delayed bank confirmations, disputes, or a result that finalizes after the HTTP call timed out, so a callback channel is needed to report them.

questions.q: What does PCI DSS scope primarily depend on?
options: The merchant's total annual payment revenue across all sales channels
Whether your systems store, process, or transmit raw card data
The number of countries where payments are accepted
Which database engine holds the transaction history
questions.explanation: Scope follows the cardholder data: any system that stores, processes, or transmits a PAN is in scope. Volume affects validation level, not which systems must be assessed.

questions.q: Why are money amounts stored as integer minor units (cents) rather than floats?
options: Integers compress far better in columnar storage
Databases cannot index floating-point columns
Binary floats can't represent many decimal amounts exactly, causing rounding drift
Currency symbols only attach cleanly to integers
questions.explanation: Values like 0.10 have no exact binary representation, so float arithmetic accumulates tiny errors that break balance invariants. Integer cents make every amount exact.

questions.q: What is authorization versus capture?
options: Auth reserves funds on the card; capture actually collects them
Auth verifies the CVV; capture verifies the billing address
Auth is the customer login step; capture is checkout
Auth happens at the bank; capture happens at the card network only
questions.explanation: Authorization places a hold confirming funds and validity, and capture later requests the actual transfer, which is why merchants can authorize at checkout and capture at shipment.

questions.q: What is tokenization of card numbers for?
options: Speeding up charge requests by shortening payloads
Generating one-time discount codes tied to a card
Detecting duplicate card numbers registered across many customer accounts
Replacing the PAN with a reference so systems avoid storing card data
questions.explanation: A token is a meaningless reference the PSP can map back to the card, so a breach of merchant systems yields nothing usable and PCI scope shrinks dramatically.

questions.q: A charge request times out. The client retries with the same idempotency key. The first attempt actually succeeded. What should the server return?
options: A brand-new charge, since the network failure voided the first attempt
An error instructing the client to check back tomorrow
The stored result of the original charge, without charging again
A partial refund covering the accidental second attempt
questions.explanation: The server recorded the outcome under that key, so replaying the stored response makes the retry a safe no-op and gives the client the answer it lost to the timeout.

questions.q: Why must webhook handlers be idempotent?
options: Webhook payloads arrive unsigned, so duplicate deliveries indicate possible tampering
PSPs may deliver the same event multiple times, especially around retries
Handlers run on multiple threads sharing one connection
Events always arrive in order, so replays are the only risk
questions.explanation: Webhook delivery is at-least-once: a slow or failed acknowledgement triggers redelivery, so processing the same event ID twice must not credit an account twice.

questions.q: Your ledger says the customer paid; the PSP report says the charge failed. Which process is designed to catch exactly this?
options: Chargeback representment through the card network
Real-time fraud scoring on the charge attempt
Quarterly PCI compliance audits covering the settlement pipeline
Reconciliation: comparing internal records against PSP settlement files
questions.explanation: Reconciliation systematically matches internal ledger entries against the PSP's authoritative settlement file and surfaces every disagreement as an exception to investigate.

questions.q: An order service must charge a card and mark the order paid, across two systems. Which pattern avoids charging without recording (or vice versa)?
options: Record intent first, then charge, then finalize, with recovery for each gap
Wrap the PSP call and the database write in one XA transaction
Charge first, then write the order row with retries until success
Use a message queue so that the charge and the database write happen simultaneously
questions.explanation: Persisting a pending intent before calling the PSP means any crash leaves a record a recovery job can query and resolve. An external PSP cannot enlist in an XA transaction.

questions.q: Why should refunds reference the original charge rather than issue a fresh opposite-direction transfer?
options: The PSP ties the refund to the charge for fees, disputes, and card routing
Opposite-direction transfers require the merchant to hold a separate money-transmitter license
Fresh transfers cannot carry negative amounts in most APIs
Refund latency is lower because no bank is involved
questions.explanation: A linked refund returns funds to the exact card used, caps the amount at what was captured, reverses fees correctly, and gives dispute handling a clear audit trail.

questions.q: A balance is stored as a single mutable column, updated in place. What key auditability property is lost versus an append-only ledger?
options: The ability to shard customer balances horizontally across multiple regions
Sub-millisecond reads of the current balance
Compatibility with double-precision arithmetic
Reconstructing how and why the balance reached its current value
questions.explanation: Overwriting discards history, so you cannot replay entries to explain or verify the number. An append-only ledger derives the balance from immutable entries you can always re-sum.

questions.q: Payments must survive a region outage. Which component is hardest to make active-active, and why?
options: The API gateway, because TLS certificates are region-bound
The ledger, because double-spend prevention needs a single source of truth per account
The webhook receiver, because PSPs only sign one endpoint
The fraud model, because feature stores cannot replicate
questions.explanation: Balance checks demand linearizable writes per account; concurrent multi-region writes could each approve a spend against the same funds, so the ledger needs a single authoritative writer.

questions.q: Retrying a failed PSP call safely requires the retry to be:
options: Executed within the same TCP connection as the original
Routed to a different PSP to avoid duplicate detection
Sent with the same idempotency key and identical request parameters
Delayed until the nightly reconciliation batch has confirmed the failure
questions.explanation: The key identifies the operation and matching parameters prove it is the same request, so the PSP can dedupe. Changing the amount under a reused key is typically rejected outright.

questions.q: Design review: idempotency keys are stored with a 24-hour TTL. A client retries a timed-out charge 25 hours later. What's the failure mode?
options: The retry is rejected because the key's cryptographic signature has expired
The key is gone, so the retry creates a second, duplicate charge
The PSP's own dedupe window guarantees safety regardless
The ledger blocks the retry via its balanced-entry invariant
questions.explanation: Once the dedupe record is evicted the key looks brand new, so the server executes the charge a second time. Retention must exceed the longest realistic client retry window.

questions.q: Under load, two workers process the same 'payment_succeeded' webhook concurrently. Idempotent handlers still double-credit. What's the likely bug?
options: The PSP signed both deliveries with different keys
TTL expiry on the dedupe record between the two reads
Check-then-insert without a unique constraint: both saw 'not processed' and proceeded
Webhook payload compression corrupted the event ID
questions.explanation: Read-then-write dedupe has a race window; only an atomic guard such as a unique index on the event ID, or an insert-first pattern, makes exactly one worker win.

questions.q: Daily reconciliation finds 0.01% of transactions mismatched. Volumes are 10M/day. What's the sound operational design?
options: Ignore mismatches below 0.1% as statistical noise
Halt all payments until each mismatch is resolved
Automatically adjust the internal ledger to match the PSP's reported numbers
Queue the ~1,000 exceptions into a workflow with alerting and aging SLAs
questions.explanation: Mismatches are real money and never noise, but they also should not stop the business, so they go into a tracked exception queue with ownership and age limits. Auto-adjusting the ledger hides genuine bugs.

questions.q: To shrink PCI scope, card data entry is moved to PSP-hosted fields (iframe or redirect). What is the resulting architecture property?
options: Raw PANs never touch your servers; you handle only tokens
Your servers store PANs encrypted, halving audit requirements
The PSP assumes liability for all fraud on your platform
Your frontend must be certified, but backends fall out of scope
questions.explanation: The card is typed into the PSP's own origin, so your backend only ever sees a token, which removes those systems from cardholder-data scope. Fraud liability is unchanged by this.
